messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When Dara was first stalked, it began in the ordinary spaces of his working life. At 50, a divorced Cambodian American musician, he was used to late nights loading equipment after sets, greeting strangers after performances, and moving between bars, rehearsal rooms, and small venues across the city. The man first appeared after a show, standing too long near the stage door, then outside Dara’s apartment building, then again at a grocery store several neighborhoods away. Over the next weeks the encounters took on a terrible pattern: repeated messages from unknown numbers, gifts left where he would find them, footsteps behind him after midnight when he carried his instrument case to his car. One night, after a performance, Dara saw the man waiting across the street under a flickering light, not approaching, just watching. Dara remembered hurrying to unlock his car while hearing his own breathing and the scrape of shoes on pavement behind him. After that night, parts of what happened blurred. He could recall the glare of the streetlight on the windshield, the smell of stale beer from the alley, and the sensation that someone was close enough to touch him, but there were stretches he simply could not retrieve no matter how hard he tried.

What hardened the experience into something ongoing was not only the stalking itself but Dara’s conviction that no one who should have protected him really did. He reported the incidents and felt brushed off, as if repeated surveillance and unwanted contact did not count until something worse happened. He had come to believe that institutions had failed him, and that belief quickly became personal: if he could not stop this, if he kept freezing and second-guessing himself, then maybe he was a weak person. From there, his world narrowed. He began avoiding unfamiliar places because he felt he could not judge danger there, and at gigs in new venues he would scan exits, doorways, and the faces in the crowd instead of settling into the music. At night, especially after performances, he found it much harder to feel safe at all. He watched other people closely for signs that they might harm him, certain that letting his guard down would mean missing the next threat.

Those same beliefs also shaped the way the stalking lived in his mind. When he tried to remember clearly, the missing pieces seemed to confirm his sense that he had failed in some basic way; he told himself a stronger man would know exactly what happened and what to do about it. His anger that nobody had stepped in left him going back over the worst moments, but not in a coherent story. Instead the memory returned in sudden shards: the glow of a phone screen in the dark, footsteps matching his pace, a figure across the street. At other times it hit with full force, as though the event were happening again in the present, complete across sight, sound, and body sensation. The vividness frightened him, but the gaps frightened him too, because both seemed like proof that the experience had gotten inside him and changed him.

As the months passed, the memory itself began to organize his days. A stranger lingering too long near a club entrance or someone walking behind him after a set could bring back the sensory reliving at once, and once that happened Dara became even more vigilant. He monitored every face, every movement of a hand into a pocket, every pause outside a backstage door. He stopped accepting bookings in unfamiliar neighborhoods and would only agree to play in venues he knew well, often asking staff to walk him to his car. These habits cost him work. Other musicians noticed he was distracted and rigid, more preoccupied with the room than with rehearsal, and he turned down collaborative opportunities if they involved new spaces or late-night travel.

The cycle tightened further because his vigilance kept the stalking present. Nights were the worst: lying awake listening for sounds in the hallway, he would catch a fragment of memory without warning, and his body would react as though the man were outside again. Watching other people so closely during the day left him keyed up and exhausted, and in that strained state the old scenes broke through more easily and more vividly. Each time this happened, Dara felt more dead inside afterward. He described an emptiness that was almost worse than fear, as if he had gone numb in order to keep functioning. That numbness fed his belief that something essential in him had been damaged, and when he saw himself as weakened and unprotected, he became even less able to relax his guard.

By the time he sought help, Dara’s life had constricted to a small circuit of familiar venues, daytime errands, and careful routes home. He still played music, but the pleasure had thinned; he spent performances studying the audience for danger and nights listening for pursuit. What finally brought him in was a recent episode after a show when a man in the parking lot glanced at him twice and Dara was suddenly back under that streetlight, heart pounding, senses flooded, unable to tell how much of what he was seeing belonged to now and how much belonged to then. He said he was tired of living as if threat were always one step behind him, but what frightened him most was the possibility that he was right to stay this alert—that if he stopped watching, no one would protect him, and the next time he might not get away.
